utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Please be seated. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning to the Registry; good morning to the counsel for the Prosecution and for the Defence; good morning, Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to continue with your cross-examination. I wish to remind you that you are continuing under oath. I don't have to explain that because you know that very well. I will give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, when was the last time you saw Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in the course of 1992, perhaps once or twice. Maybe also in 1993 twice. I saw him very few times in all the years that went by until my arrest. A couple of times only throughout that whole period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you see him in either 1995 or 1996?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have in passing. We may have passed one another and greeted one another, but I cannot say for sure. I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you see him after a time you were both indicted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is he today? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know he has a socially-owned apartment in Omarska, that is what I heard, because in 1992 he wasn't living in that apartment. But I later heard that he had that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated on page 4 of the interview that has the -- it bears the name of the author Christopher Bennett. It is 3/201. On page 4 of that interview, you were asked -- have you found it, Mr. Kvocka? Do you have your copy in your language?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the interview. I tried to keep it as a memento but the ladies from the Registry took it away from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sure we'll get one in just a moment. If you can find the section which discusses why you left Omarska, it is on page 4 of the English version. If you're able to locate it, I'd appreciate it if you'd let me know when you've found it. You were asked, "Why did you leave Omarska in June?" Have you found it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Why did you leave Omarska in June?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just like I was appointed, people from my station told me that I was to be transferred to another post. The formulation used in the police is "transferred in accordance with the needs of the service. And then you were asked:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you perhaps relieved of office because you complained because of what was happening in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I complained specifically to no one. If I was present when excesses occurred, I would prevent them and ask for a regular investigation to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you think that this is the reason you were replaced?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I do not know. I never even inquired as a matter of principle. In fact, I think they did me a big favour. Tukovi --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, there is a lack of precision in many places here. The wording is quite different. Here it says, "Why did you leave Omarska?" The answer doesn't follow, just like I was appointed. I think the phrasing is rather strange, but I don't think that is important. I think I will be able to respond. The question was probably, "How did you leave? How did you go away from Omarska?" And I said in the same way as I got there, which means my superior can determine where I am to work. Similarly, he can say, "You're no longer going to work there." Because of the needs of the service, superiors are not obliged to give any extensive explanations, so they simply say that the needs of the service require that you go to work in another location. Not a different workplace, just a different location. So I wanted to point out that there was a lack of precision. Here it says I did not complain to anyone in particular because my principle was not to ask any questions, any additional explanations if I am given an order to do something. But I think that the substance is not affected by this lack of precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then the substance being that it was an administrative transfer, not a punitive transfer, correct? Strictly administrative, needs of service, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be described in that way in the context of the explanations I have just given. The superior would simply say, "You're going to work there." I don't understand the difference between administrative and non-administrative or punitive. I simply had to obey, and I did, and I didn't want to inquire about the reasons. If I had inquired, it is highly questionable what the response would have been. "Why are you asking? It's more or less none of your business. I am the one who will decide where you work."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tukovi, you indicated in your testimony, was a small reserve station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just so that all of us have a clear picture of what the reserve station concept means, I would ask the usher kindly to distribute 3/209. It is a document from the Prijedor collections, a police station document. And mindful of the Chamber's wish to have authentication issues resolved, I'm waiting for the individual who was the leader of the search to return, and I shall provide a written summary of locations of seizure. If the usher has an extra -- no, it's okay. One for the ELMO. That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you clearly see in front of you, Mr. Kvocka, what is called "Receipt For Solemn Oaths Taken," and it --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the purpose for which I'd like to ask you to look at this document is it lists reserve police stations using the initials "RSM," and the stations are broken down into ten stations. The first being Prijedor I, the second Prijedor II, the third being Omarska RSM, the fourth Lamovita, the fifth Rakelici, the sixth Gomjenica, the seventh Brezicani, eighth Cikote, ninth Tukovi. So Tukovi and Omarska have the same status in terms of what they are; would you agree? They are reserve police stations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, although the numbers perhaps of staff may be different, they are nonetheless, as we both agree, reserve police stations. That's what they have in common. The difference I would like to ask you about, and I would ask you if you can tell me what you know about the cleansing of an area known as Brdo. Are you familiar with Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. As a name, I know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which municipalities are included in that title, Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brdo is part of Prijedor municipality, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I stand corrected. You're absolutely right. I meant which villages, I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several villages. I may know some of them, but I did not move around much in the area, or rather, I never did, except in 1977 and 1978 where I went on patrol there at the beginning of my career as a policeman. But there were villages there such as Biscani and Rizvanovici, Zecovi, Rasavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How about Carakovo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Carakovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how about Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And Hambarine was the location where in May there was the checkpoint incident; is that right? That's the same Hambarine? Is that correct, Mr. Kvocka? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That was, was it not, essentially the last, as it were, Muslim stronghold in terms of population that had not been cleansed as of the time you transferred to Tukovi. There were still quite a few Muslims living in those villages, were there not, at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite agree. I think there were some activities prior to that. About the 20th of May were the incidents in Hambarine, after the operation, Hambarine, Biscani, Rasavci, I think that the operations were already over. However, Rasavci, and Zecovi were populated by majority Serb population. Rasavci is almost totally Serb, and Zecovi had a mixed population, as far as I can remember from what I knew in 1977, 1978.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you not agree that, let's say roughly the 23rd, 24th of July, 1992, certain villages including Carakovo were cleansed of whatever Muslim population remained, and they were cleansed either by way of murder or removal to various camps. You would know about that; you were in Tukovi at the time. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember that the Red Cross, at a stadium which was not completed, transported a certain number of people. The stadium was still under construction. They were transported in the direction of Travnik; that is, I'm not quite sure where. But I do remember that. This was something of general knowledge in Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were working --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I also remember that an interventions platoon had some activities in that connection. An intervention platoon, I'm not quite sure which unit it belonged to, but it did belong to the public security station in Prijedor. I think it was not part of the police station structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A Serb intervention platoon, you're saying? Part of the Serb institutions' intervention platoon from --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were working regular hours at that point in time, as I understand it. You were working a regular, full-time, active-duty position once you got to Tukovi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in Tukovi when this event that the Red Cross organised took place. At that time I was in Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When do you say the Red Cross event took place, please? When do you date that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in July, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, that was the local --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been seven, eight, or ten days, or maybe even 15 days after I arrived there. I cannot be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is the local Red Cross, correct, not the International Red Cross? This was a local Red Cross unit; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Red Cross of Prijedor. In those days, we never had occasion to see the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What date do you put your arrival for work at the Tukovi Police Station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From everything that I learnt about during the proceedings and the documents tendered by yourself and the Defence, I am able to assert that it was the 1st of July, though before that I couldn't be quite precise. It could have been a day earlier or a day later. Afterwards, when I look back and analyse things more closely, I do know that that was the date, that is, the 1st of July. I'm sure about that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher, please, to distribute Prosecution's 3/189.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, the document which you have before you - also, Your Honours, from the Prijedor seizures - is a record from the Public Security Station Prijedor concerning salaries and personnel records from 29 June 1992. On this document, there are the names of various police personnel, including Jankovic, as you can see, Brane Bolta. I'm leafing through it trying to get to your name. And then on -- I'm sorry. I'm leafing too fast. I beg your pardon, Your Honours. It's page -- well, actually, it has a "1" at the bottom, but in the upper right-hand corner, it says 01907797. You are listed as number 1 on that particular grid. Do you see it Mr. Kvocka? I'm sorry if I go too fast. The upper right-hand corner of yours may have a different number.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It lists your personnel number and then it has points which I do not understand. But what it has that I want to just confirm with you is hours. It has your hours for the month of June 1992 as 184 hours, and it's the same number of hours that show for Zeljko Meakic, for Ljuban Grahovac, for Mladjo Radic, for Milutin Vujic. There seems to be a standard number of hours for having worked the month of June. That would represent, would it not, a full-time activity on the work schedule for the month of June? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was between 182 and 184 hours. This was permitted by law. But in the police it was possible to work a couple hours longer. Because of the limit set by law, overtime is not paid in the police in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: However, everybody who was working that month in these positions had 184 hours, and you're one of those persons. Okay. There's no indication, I note, for any type of leave. That appears to represent actual hours worked, if I'm correct. That represents actual hours worked, real hours.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if a commander gave somebody a day off, then the number of hours would not be reduced accordingly. If you have something that you need to do, a private obligation, and you ask your commander for a day off and he grants you that day off, that would not affect your salary. The commander had the right to give you this day off, free day, without reducing the number of hours, the number of working hours, precisely because of what I just said. Sometimes you would have to work overtime, in which case, again, the number of working hours would not go up. That would not be reflected here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But these hours, 184 hours, reflect the number of hours you would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have worked on your 12-hour shifts times whatever number of days; would that be a fair way of calculating 184? I'm not sure how they did the arithmetic, but that it represents all hours worked on all shifts that you had; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to clarify something. This is a report to the accounting service, the finance service, for them to be able to pay out your salary, and that is why you see here that all the workers have an equal number of hours. But I'm quite certain that in reality the number of hours differed for each of these workers. The actual number of hours spent at work can be seen from other records but not from this record, which is intended to the accounting service for the payment of salaries. The commander puts down 184 hours for each one so that everyone can get his full salary. He will not increase the number of hours because that would not be remunerated, nor will he decrease the number of hours. Exceptionally, if there was certified sick-leave which was longer than seven days, then that would be indicated on this list and the number of hours would be reduced accordingly. So this is an ordinary report for salaries. The commander simply indicates that every worker performed his duties during the month, not counting one, two, or three days that he may have given him as free days, nor does he indicate any increase in the number of hours because that will not be reflected in the salary. There would not be an appropriate increase in the salary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I note, Mr. Kvocka, that on some of the earlier pages before we get to your name, there are some indications -- for example, on the fourth page in, I notice that, for example, a Mr. Milorad Macura has 92 hours down, not 184. His name appears two persons below the name Brane Cvijic, whom we've talked about as one of the persons who arrested Fikret Kadiric, if you recall. Now, there is some variation on different pages. Not everybody has 184 hours. So perhaps there's a bookkeeping secret neither of us knows. But it's not for everybody; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows exactly what I was just saying. Macura probably worked for half the month; the other half he was either on sick-leave or on annual leave. That's why he has 92 hours. It's the exact half of 184. So he didn't work for half a month and that has to be reflected. Because if he was on sick-leave, then somebody else makes up for the difference in his salary, that is, social insurance will compensate him, because this is a drastic reduction in the number of hours and that has to be recorded. I said that if it was one, two, or three days, that is, ten hours up or down, that would not be reflected, at least as far as I know from practice. Some commanders may have been more particular than others in their records. In any event, if the commander granted leave for somebody to be off for a day, he will not reduce the number of hours; but if somebody failed to turn up at work without permission, then the number of hours would be reduced. So that is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So are you suggesting that you can work 45 hours fewer than are required and still be listed as being there full time? Is that what you're telling us? If you work three-quarters of the month, you indicated you could essentially with less than seven days or fewer than seven days, get away without having it recorded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I am saying that if the commander gave you two or three days off at his own initiative, and he has the right to do that - I think it is specified up to three days - in that case he would not reduce the number of hours for the purpose of salaries because this has to do with the payment of salaries. However, in certain other records, such as perhaps the roll-call paper, then it would be indicated clearly that I hadn't worked on that day. A traffic accident may occur, and you are on the list as working whereas in your free time you had an accident, this could have serious consequences. So there are other records which show exactly who worked on what day and who was off. But this is a report for salaries, and if the commander gave you one, two, or three days off - I can't remember exactly how many days he had the right to give you, according to the internal regulations I think it was a maximum of three days - then the hours counted for your salary would not be reduced because he could count on you that another month you would work ten hours extra, so then it would mean 200 hours. But as I said, since overtime in the police is not remunerated, then in these reports for salaries, 184 is written as a rule, if there is no annual leave or sick leave longer than seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And so how would a commander or how would a person from the Prijedor police department many years later be able to look at records like this and determine, for example, that you were out for seven days during the last week of June? On what would that person base it if it's not indicated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I think we are turning around in a circle. I think that Mr. Kvocka will tell you that there was another record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a feeling we're repeating things, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate, Your Honour, and I'm sure you, I'm sure you're correct. And I'd like him to tell me that there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, how would a person six, seven, eight years later be able to say, "Oh, yes, he was out during those days," if it's not reflected? Explain it, please, what type of records.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a document called Narodni list, or work schedule, and the worker in the administration in the police station, not in the department but in the police station, he keeps a record. And every two or three days he collects all the daily schedules of the whole service and enters this in this global work schedule. And then from this schedule one can see exactly who worked when, from what time until what time, what type of service, patrol, security, traffic control, or something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. You were only one of two active-duty police officers to be stationed at Tukovi; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at first. I think another person came, Macura, Dragan, but not this one, not -- oh, it may be this one, Milorad Macura. He came to Tukovi sometime after me, maybe ten or 15 days later. And if you are thinking of Lazo Basrak, he was an active duty policeman; however, he was still not employed in Prijedor, so he was treated as a reserve policeman. So he was a professional, but as he came from Zagreb, he still did not have permanent employment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And so you were sent to Tukovi to be an assistant to the chief then, the commander then, Milodrag, is that his name, Drazic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drazic, yes. He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you were sent to be his assistant?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, do not respond because this is a blatant example of a leading question. "You were sent to be his assistant," that was what my learned colleague said. At least, that was the translation I received. You were sent there to be an assistant to Mr. Mile Drazic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Kvocka was going to answer the question. Do not worry about him. He knows how to answer questions that are being put to him. At any rate, there are leading questions and leading questions. There is also a difference. Mr. Kvocka was going to answer the question calmly with no problem whatsoever. I am sure about that. Ms. Somers, would you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You went there, you were sent there, to be his assistant, as your wife told us in her testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my wife doesn't have a clue when it comes to the work of a police. I said in an interview, in this interview with Bob Reid or someone else - I'm sure you will be able to find it - that on that morning when I was able to find Jankovic to see what was going to happen with me, he told me -- at least, my impression was that he wanted to calm down the tension that had developed between the two of us over the past several days. He said, "Go to Tukovi, report to Mile Drazic, and help him with the records at the station because there's no one there who is able to do that, who is able to draft an official note," for example, which is, which is one of the most simple things in the police. An official note is something that contains official information on the basis of which further work is necessary. I may have said to Bennett, Chris, that I went there to work as some kind of assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think you're right. If you look at page 6 of your interview in the English, and I'm sorry, I don't have a B/C/S edition --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it by heart.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But on page 6 of the Bennett interview:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What happened to you after you left Omarska? What did you do from then on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assistant commanding officer in a wartime police station, a reserve police station, in a place --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I do apologise. As, as an assistant. That's what it says in my translation. Please, do not skip it. I think the same wording is used in your text. I was as an assistant to the commander in a police station, in a reserve police station. We are again confusing the same thing as we did yesterday. In a neighbourhood in Prijedor, at the outskirts of Prijedor, that was the answer that I gave, and that's what it is stated here. I couldn't come to terms to what was happening with me, so -- well, I was some kind of assistant. I stayed in the service. And my wife, she knew that I was the leader of the sector in Omarska department. When she was speaking about that, what she had in mind was the fact that I was the chief of the sector in Omarska, and then all of a sudden I become an assistant of the sector leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: (redacted) who indicated that you returned to Omarska camp three times a week roughly, every third day, until the 6th of August. That suggests, does it not, you had a fair amount of liberty, discretion, as to how to structure your day when you were at Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know who said that, two or three times a week until August, (redacted), I don't know who you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. The transcript has the wrong name. It should read (redacted) for correction, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kvocka, I didn't mean to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his testimony about those details exactly. I remember that he said that he used to see me in Omarska after his arrest, and my testimony was, and I -- that is what I said on a couple of occasions, both to the journalists, your investigators, and during my testimony here, that I had left two or three times from Omarska during that first week. Now, I know that I left on two or three occasions, and once again after the 1st of July while I was still in Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe you yourself indicated you had come back to see your brothers-in-law. You also indicated in your direct examination that one of your wife's relatives who lived in one of the villages - I'm trying to think of it, it begins with an "A," - needed some assistance, and you were able to commandeer a truck, a driver, some petrol while you were at Tukovi and render the assistance and get these people to safety through what you described as great risk. Again, you seem to have enough latitude from your job --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- to do that. When did you leave Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not talking about an important position that I had there. I did it because I felt like I should do it. I worked in Tukovi in a building which has only one small office with an iron bed where Mile Drazic as an elderly man slept. And there was a telephone indeed, and on one occasion my wife did call, and she told me that the Alisic people, our cousins, had called me. They live in the Alisici village towards the direction of Sanski Most, at the very border of the two municipalities, Sanski Most and Prijedor. They said there was shooting going on in their area, shelling as well, that they didn't know what to do. I said, "I will be home shortly and then we will see what we are going to do." And within one hour or two hours I think we found a truck, fuel. There was a person by the name of Mijatovic who was a driver. He was in Prijedor with a small truck. We found him, but he was afraid to go there, and I said, "I will go as well." And then happen what may, my wife also went with them. I was not in the truck with them. I was ahead of them in a small -- in a white Golf which had been requisitioned in Tukovi at the reserve police station. So I drove ahead of him in that Golf, and we went to Alisici. We took them in. There was an elderly woman there and her cousin, Alisic, together with his wife and two children. They had already prepared some sacks of potatoes and I don't know what else. We put everything in the truck, and I advised them to lie down on the bottom of the truck. And it is from there that we went to Prijedor and arrived in the house of my in-laws. And in Prijedor, we realised that the canvas had some bullet holes, the canvas which was on top of the part of the truck which was used for the transport of goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This was while you were working as a police officer in --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a police officer in Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just reminding you that in your interview with Investigator Reid, on page 124, and that would be in your document -- sorry, just a second, please. Bear with me. Page 131 to 132, that is, 131 to 132 in Serbo-Croat. Investigator Reid, on page 124, asks you:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what position did you hold at this reserve police station in Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jankovic told me that I was to assist in the work because Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there was only one other professional policeman there and there was nobody else, no other professional policeman. The others were reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you were to assist the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I just told you about. That's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The cleansing of villages such as Carakovo, when that occurs and there are people who are arrested, your police station at Tukovi is on the road that these people would have to be taken along if they were going to go to camps, would they not? Is that not correct? Tukovi is the closest police station to the Brdo area.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, how many persons from the various villages that you enumerated were arrested through the cleansing process in late July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those operations which were conducted at that time in that area - we can call them cleansing, I don't know exactly what it was; there was shooting going on that could be heard - they were conducted by the military. According to the information, police information, that I had, because I'm curious by nature, the military police and an intervention platoon also took part in those operations. The intervention platoon which, according to my assessment and knowledge, was under the direct command of Simo Drljaca. It was the intervention platoon of the MUP, the police station. So those sections of the police took part in that, the military police and the intervention platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It was necessary, was it not, to have a well-staffed police station to be available for eventualities arising from this cleansing process; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. It was not necessary for the police to do anything there. It was the military command which conducted military operations. The reserve police has nothing to do with that. They did not take part in those operations, nor could they participate. The military command - I don't know exactly which one, maybe the 43rd or 343rd, as it was called at that time, Motorised Brigade - together with a portion of the military police, and according to what I could observe, the intervention platoon also took part in that. If military operations are conducted in a given area, the police does not interfere. They cannot interfere; they are prohibited from interfering. Those are military operations. I'm talking about wartime conditions and not peacetime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca was a member of the police structure, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wonder if I might ask for just a moment of private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, without repeating those names, do you recall going with those two individuals back to Carakovo, however it's pronounced, to dig up the wealth that had been left behind by these Muslims who had to flee? You were in your police uniform or your military uniform and Ckalja was in his police uniform. You found the gold jewellery after the woman returned with her brother and you gave back the watch of the husband who was brutally murdered in front of the woman's eyes. You don't remember that event?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I remember how it went. I will tell you all about it, but it was not the way you described it. There were no murders whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I'm not suggesting you had anything -- that you were involved in the murder. The murder occurred when the Serb soldiers cleansed that village in 1992. However, you did know, as did Ckalja, that it was a village of some wealth and that's why you went back there with that man --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Explain why the gold was divided between you and Ckalja.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't divide it. Let us be clear about that right away. It is possible that the event happened in 1993 or maybe 1994. Maybe you have more precise information about that, but that is not important. It was Ckalja who came to me in Prijedor and he told me that he had a very good friend who had to dig up something that had been hidden, and he asked me whether we could help him. I told him that we could. So we went there but not in a blue Lada, in a Zastava 101, which belonged to my kum, Hasan Oklopcic. It was his car. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went there but he wasn't quite sure about where it was. So we went back to Prijedor and he said that he would contact someone by telephone who was living abroad at the time so that the person would explain to him the exact location of the place. After awhile, the two of them came to me again, saying that they had some more reliable information now. When we went there on the second occasion, he did find a jar with a golden watch, two or three rings, and one golden chain, and he took it. I don't know what happened with those things afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Don't you remember telling him to take back the broken watch that belonged to the murdered man, give it to his widow, and to give her the worthless items, and you kept the gold? You don't remember that? You otherwise seem to recall quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. That man, the man by the surname that we just mentioned - I don't want to mention it again - he was the one who took those items. I don't know who the items belonged to and to whom he was supposed to give it back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on. Women in Omarska camp, how many women were there altogether, as far as you know, in Omarska camp during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 15 and 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were they doing in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were detainees there. They were considered to be detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were they doing? What was their task in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have any tasks. They would sit down there in the restaurant, in one of the corners, and that is where I would usually see them. From time to time, one, two, or three of them would wash the dishes in the area where the food was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your interview, on page 9, the Bennett -- the one marked Bennett, page 9, you are asked about women. English page 9. I'm sorry, I do not know the B/C/S page. You are asked:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In connection with the evidence that some women were locked up, maltreated, and raped at Omarska, what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only that there was a certain number of women there. I do not know how many exactly. Some 20 of them. I know that they were separated from the other prisoners, to call them that, and their conditions of accommodation were much better than for the others because they were women. I knew some of them personally before the war. If they complained of boredom, they were allowed to work a bit in the kitchen, help with the washing up and distribution of food. Please tell me how often and who complained to you of boredom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). She was a kind of woman -- she was very lively, if I can use that expression. She was very active. She kept walking up and down the restaurant, complaining of boredom, and she would ask if there was any kind of work that she could do. She kept laughing, asking for cigarettes, and saying, "Is there anything one can do here? I'm bored to death."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I note that in your interview with Investigator Reid you made no mention of your brother Zoran Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned him somewhere but I'm not sure. He didn't ask me anything about that. But I will tell you everything you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me just amend my comment to you. I should apologise in that you didn't mention that your brother, whose name was Lija, is that what you told us in court? Lija was his nickname?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my brother's name is Lija.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That Lija was at Omarska for at least -- at least one night that you were there. He told us that in court; you didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention that he had been there, and I don't think he said that either. He didn't say that he was there at the time I was there. I don't know whether you are doing it on purpose, but you're misinterpreting. He talked about his arrival there at the beginning of the work of the investigations centre, and he also spoke about people being detained. He never said at any point in time that I was there, nor was I able to tell Bob Reid anything about him because I did not know anything. It was prior to his testimony that I actually learned that he was there on the first night, on the 27th or 28th, at the beginning of the work of the investigations centre. I don't know exactly what they did. You are misinterpreting things, and things are actually very simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: He was also a guard, or at least he had access to the detainees, didn't he, at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, no. There were guards. Milojica, Zoran, and Miroslav Kvocka, those were the three people who were guards. And Zoran, son of Gorcin, from the village of Maricka, who was killed at the front in Gradacac in the month of November or December 1992, that is Zoran Kvocka who was a guard -- he was a guard at the Omarska. As regards Zoran Kvocka, called Lija, my own brother was not a guard in the Omarska camp. You can easily find out about that if you have a look at your documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Whether or not he was an official guard, he was in the camp on a number of occasions, was he not, abusing inmates, detainees. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the kind of knowledge that you have. However, what I know is something that I heard from him that I didn't know from before, that on one occasion he brought cigarettes to my brothers-in-law. And here I heard that he was there on the first night together with Cigo. So don't make me repeat his testimony here; you have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yesterday we saw a document that you helped us identify as one that lists the title of wartime police station Omarska, and it had the names of various persons who were to be given passes to get in. And on that list, I believe at the bottom under the cooks section, kitchen transport related, was a name --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka's cross-examination has been going on for ten hours and more, and I would request that my learned friend shows the document to Mr. Kvocka so that he can follow what she's talking about. We have seen so many documents. He can't remember everything. He can't have everything in his mind, so that would speed things up and facilitate understanding if he's given a copy of the document she's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. You mentioned the time, and we have to calculate also the time spent on your interventions. Mr. Kvocka did not complain that he wants to have the document. You are a very, very attentive lawyer, but give some space to your witness as well. So Ms. Susan Somers, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yesterday's document, just so that the Chamber and document are aware, was 3/208, and on it was the name Dzervida, D with a little line through it, e-r-v-i-d-a, as someone who worked in the kitchen area as a cook or a bread deliverer, I'm not quite clear, but it was related to food, in Omarska camp. I would ask the usher kindly to distribute 3/199.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what you have in front of you, if you've received it, first of all the top page of it, which I believe may only be in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbo-Croat, is a document which indicates that a Tribunal representative, who signed his name as William A. Studenar, received certain documents from the Bosnian government in Bihac, and among those documents is a document bearing the number of 0212716/94, as is indicated on the face of that document, and also 0212715/94. The document appears to be a statement as well as -- actually, a statement in two forms. One is a summary report and the other is background information with -- one of the documents in the original language bears a signature of the person Dzervida as well as the people who conducted -- took the statement. This date is a date before your indictment. It was 1994. And the individual Dzervida, who calls him Drasko in this particular report, is a Serb who was captured by the Bosniaks and was giving information. In the document on the second page, he talks a bit about himself and you. I'm sorry, second page talks about your brother Zoran, but he talks about you as well. As to Zoran on the second page of the document he says, "Cigo is a sabotage group, the commander of which was Momcilo Rade Kovic called Cigo." And he goes on to describe him. "The following were members of his group, Zoran Kvocka called Lija, from the village of Maricka," and he names people. "Zoran Kvocka is tall, balding, and about 30 years old. Cigo's group took part in the looting together with the Maniakosi," I hope I'm pronouncing it right. "They burned houses, killed, expelled the population from Lenic and took them to the camps. People from Prijedor and the surrounding villages were taken to Omarska --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object, regardless of the time. Is the purpose here for Ms. Somers to read to us the statement? And I must point out straight away, in the statement before us we don't see the signature of Dzervida. Shouldn't she ask the witness about this statement, or is the purpose to enter this whole statement into the transcript, which is a pattern that is repeating itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, what is the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only trying to link the passages about Zoran Kvocka, and on the next page, the top paragraph of the last page, about Miroslav Kvocka. I do not wish -- certainly do not wish to take the Chamber's time in reading it. And it is unlikely, Your Honours, that this individual would have seen this document. It's the information contained in it that I would like to ask about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have an objection, Your Honour, and it's based on the previous rulings of this Chamber, and Your Honours have ruled that during cross-examination it is unfair and not permitted to put someone else's statement to a witness during cross-examination based on what someone else may have said. And indeed, Your Honours have ruled that during cross-examination, we cannot put to a witness what a previous Prosecution witness has said about certain events. And certainly it is unfair and inappropriate to put what purports to be a statement by someone else for this witness to comment on. Your Honours have ruled that way in the past, and I submit that that ruling should be followed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are right, but the Chamber ruled that the parties could use in the cross-examination things to clarify a contradiction or check the credibility of the witness. The documents may be used but will not be admitted into evidence. This came as a result of a whole series of discussions that we had. Therefore, Ms. Susan Somers, I think the point is, you have to choose: Either you read the document and not tender it, or you ask for it to be tendered. I'm sorry, I seem to have lost, to have got lost. The ruling of the Chamber was that prior statements, including statements given to other authorities, are not admitted into evidence. However, they may be used to impeach the witness or to clarify a contradiction. So if you're using the document, you're not going to tender it into evidence. So it's up to you to choose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With respect, previous statements given by the witness can be used in the way you just described, but in my submission, we're talking about a statement given by somebody else, that's purportedly given by somebody else. By a third person. And precisely you have not allowed us to put to successive Prosecution witnesses what a previous Prosecution witness stated on the basis of fairness and appropriateness to the witness testifying. This is not a statement that purports to come from Mr. Kvocka, a previous statement from him. This is from a third person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think we have to speed things up and get to your question because the question is what is important. All parties can say, "I have information that is such and such," and then put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was not going to seek the admission, but I wanted, in fairness, to at least have the documents in front of everyone so that they could see from what I was reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There is information from a particular document I would ask you to comment on. This Serb who was part of the group indicated the camp commander at Omarska, again, I have to -- I'm sorry, I have to back up a little so you know what I'm talking about. On the second page at the very bottom it indicates, "I was allocated to the 3rd Battalion of the 43rd Prijedor Brigade in the rear unit. I worked in the kitchen which prepared food for the Omarska camp. I was in charge of the bread transport from Prijedor to Omarska. The camp commander was Miroslav Kvocka who was replaced after a certain time by Zeljko Meakic." Did you know this individual Dzervida? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I'm trying to think of his face. There are at least three or four Dzervidas, and even Drasko Dzervidas. There are three or four Drasko Dzervidas in the areas of the villages of Gradina and Omarska, and it is quite possible that one of them drove bread from Prijedor to the kitchen in the iron ore mine. It's quite possible. But he said that he drove bread from Prijedor to the kitchen. He knows nothing more than that. I would like you to analyse many of the things that he has said here because I see that the man was captured, that he was talking a lot of nonsense. He just linked up some names that he happened to remember. You see, he was exchanged. I heard that he was exchanged under very difficult circumstances, and if we're talking about the same Dzervida, it's quite possible that he was never exchanged, that he's still missing. I didn't know you would ask me about this; I would have perhaps inquired. There is one Drasko Dzervida who was never exchanged, and he gave to the Muslim police or army in Bihac these statements, and subjected to such torture, he would be ready to say that he slept with his mother if that would help him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your position -- I beg your pardon, Mr. Kvocka. Your views on when a person entered Omarska camp and when a person was standing, as we might say, on the threshold of Omarska camp, are discussed between you and Investigator Reid on page 42 of the English version of your interview, which would be in your language - I'll tell you in just a second - 46 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I see that my learned friend has moved on from this document, she stated that the document was signed, regardless of what Mr. Kvocka said. But really, there is no authenticity of this document. There's no signature. So we would like to see whether Drasko Dzervida signed this document which was referred to in this examination. I'm not doubting that it was signed, but I'd like to see, us and Your Honours, to see that signature.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have here, this is not Drasko, this is AID that gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not, of course, seeking to have it admitted. There are signatures. I don't have the original, this is a copy. Let me see if I can -- my translation indicates a place on the left side, and I think in the original language it's -- I don't know how well -- it's very, very faint, but it looks to -- my B/C/S copy bears the name Dzervida Drasko, and I don't know whether or not -- I do not see -- my copy is not sufficiently clear to show anything else.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But without a signature, no signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. You can have the floor when I give you the floor. I am listening to the translation, so I cannot hear Ms. Susan Somers as well as you at the same time. So I have to say, "You have the floor." So "floor." So now you have the floor, and please remember that there are the interpreters. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. On the photocopy that I have, the signatures of the other two persons are clearly visible, but not that of Mr. Drasko Dzervida, and my learned friend said that it was signed by Mr. Dzervida, so I'm protesting. If there is no signature, then this whole passage should be redacted from the transcript; otherwise, it cannot be allowed to stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, what Ms. Susan Somers said, she said it was signed because in the translation there is mention of a name. She said that she looked at the original, and the original has a signature, and what we have is a copy. So what we need to do is for Ms. Susan Somers, tomorrow or on another day, to show to the parties the original document with the signature, that's all, that's all. And as we are going to have a Status Conference next week, we can clear this matter up when talking about documents. For the moment, Ms. Susan Somers is not going to tender this document into evidence. This is a document that will not be part of the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But Ms. Somers quoted from this document. She asked questions; she asked comments. If I am asking comments about something that is construed, that is a forgery, that is not permissible. She used this document as a valid document asking the witness to comment on it, confusing the accused. So it is not permissible to use a falsified document regardless of whether it will be tendered and admitted or not. That's what I'm saying. All we want is to see the original and to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, do you have the original with the signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have the original. If it could be that there is not one, what I am submitting to the Court is the fact that this came from the Bosnian authorities. Even unsigned, it came from the authorities. Its value can be weighed or rejected. I do not intend to submit this into evidence. I wanted to ask about certain incidents that came out of the archives of the Bosnian authorities, having captured a Serb soldier. If, in fact, the witness cannot recollect anything that was mentioned in there, so be it. I won't push the issue any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just emphasise one thing, that when you're using this technique, and I admit that it gets a bit confusing when you quote enormously long passages from a particular document, I understand you not to be, as you've reiterated, not to be seeking admission of it into evidence; though, as I say, it begins to get a little bit on the edge when you're reading paragraph after paragraph after paragraph. But what I do want to emphasise is that even though you do that, nothing - nothing - of substance in those paragraphs is anything which we can use as evidence that that really happened. The only thing that becomes evidence is what Mr. Kvocka says when he says, "That never happened; I never knew that person; that couldn't have happened; I never knew that." That's the evidence in the case, and the evidence is not anything that's read to him. We can't, in a judgement, site anything that you put in through that particular technique. That's the way I'm receiving it, in which case, the authentication becomes less important than if you were trying to admit it into evidence for the substance thereof. But I do admit it gets a little confusing when you really read -- if it were conceivable to say, "In this document, a person was captured by the Bosnians. It says that your brother went into the camp and did looting things, and in particular here are a couple of sentences. Now, what do you say about that?" and he says, "Never happened. I never heard about it," that's the evidence. Nothing that you read to him can we rely upon unless it's actually admitted into evidence. Now, that's the spirit in which I'm receiving this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is absolutely correct, Your Honour. As it was meant, I needed to give enough information to elicit a response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sometimes you give us more than enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I try to put it in the context so that there would be no confusion as to what I was referring. Yes, that is exactly correct, Your Honour, Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Judge Wald, I would like to add a point. I agree. But there is one thing, and that is that you are presenting this document and you told us that the document was signed, and that is the problem. You cannot present a document as being signed when you don't have a signature. That is the problem, after all. We have wasted a lot of time because of this, Ms. Susan Somers, and we come back to yesterday's issue. You are presenting documents, but in this particular case, we do have an explanation and the receipt indicating the source. But you should have said that the document was not signed. But when you said that it was signed, that was what caused all the confusion. So I think that now we should have a break, a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Not yet, Ms. Somers. Mr. Kos is not yet here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that we are now ready to proceed. Ms. Somers, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I was beginning to ask you about your views on when a person enters Omarska camp, and in trying to understand this, I was looking at page 42 of your interview with Investigator Reid. If I could possibly get the B/C/S number for you. English page 42; it would be 46, 47 in Serbo-Croat. A discussion that I'd like to try to get some clarification about surrounds prisoners who were getting off of buses as they were being brought to Omarska, and it begins with the question -- I'm sorry. Reid asks:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there not some of these extremists who were more extreme than the others who would need special looking after?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no clear information about that. I know that the people escorting in the beginning used to say that a certain group was particularly -- a group of particular extremists because they were caught in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When these prisoners were being taken from the buses, did you ever see cordons or lines of police and escorts lining up and the prisoners having to pass through and being beaten while they were passing through these cordons or those lines?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the beginning there were situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning. At least once.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing I could do, and should do nothing. This was done by the people who brought the prisoners, they draw them through this line or cordon, and that was it. And then they were put up as I already mentioned. And the guards went back on buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But isn't it true that these prisoners are being transferred into your custody?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot understand it that way, because the people who brought them are still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But aren't you responsible for their safety as well as part of the security, weren't they your instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that they did not actually get into the centre then yet. What I find confusing is you're telling the Chamber, interviewers as well, that you would only act if something happens before your very eyes. Those were your words, "I did not see certain things. If I had seen." Now, in this instance, you see it, but you nonetheless seem to suggest that it's still not your responsibility even when it happens in front of your eyes. Can you explain this confusion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It would take me at least half a day to do that, but I'll try to be as brief as possible. I don't know what is the most interesting part for you here, perhaps the cordons. When people were brought there in buses, it was customary for the escort to get off the bus. I'm referring to the first two days when people were brought in buses. That was the last time they were brought in buses after that. That is while I was there and according to what I know. Usually buses were coming one after the other, and then one bus would wait for another, that is, for the people to get off from the previous bus. So what would happen then was that the escort people who were on the buses, four or five of them, got off the bus, and then two or three of them would stand on each side of the door outside the bus. And the detainees getting off the bus would have to pass through between them. So that was the cordon that is referred to and that we mentioned it as such. However, what is not mentioned here is something that I can tell you about. I remember a particular event when people from this cordon forced the detainees to sing some songs which at that time were considered to be sort of nationalistic songs. The detainees were even made to slap each other at times. This is what I was able to observe on one occasion from the window of the duty office. The people who were taking those people into custody were wearing white belts, so I assumed that they were members of the military police. There were others as well, but there were quite a few of them wearing white belts. If you want me to comment on the second part, I can only give you my opinion. As long as they were not put up in rooms, they were under their jurisdiction. The detainees were under their jurisdiction before they were actually accommodated. Once they were put up in appropriate rooms, we were supposed to be in charge after that. They were our responsibility. And that is what I was trying to explain to Bob Reid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is that written, that there is an inner phase and a little grey area when people are taken off of a bus, heading toward whatever accommodation you see fit to give them, that they are not your wards upon setting foot on the grounds of Omarska camp; where is that written? Who said that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand you. There were no established lines like on a football field. People who were their escorts were responsible for them for as long as they were not put up anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is that written?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the customary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That was the custom.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where that is written. It was a practice. I'm talking about how things were in practice. There was no appropriate law on the investigation centre. Had there been such a law, I would gladly give you my comment on it, but there wasn't such a law. There was a law on the application of police rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You stood there, you watched everything you just described to us that you saw with your own eyes, watched the abuse of persons in your presence, in your presence, and you did absolutely nothing. Isn't that really what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot talk about my presence there. If I had been there -- you cannot say that I was really actually there at that moment. This took place over a period of a couple of seconds. I cannot say -- I don't know whether you can call that singing torture, torturing of people. I don't know if it was really necessary for me to get organised, so to speak, and to enter into a conflict with the military police if they were forcing those people to sing songs. This lasted for a minute or two. I don't know what kind of intervention one could expect from anyone at that moment with a view of preventing it. I don't know what would be a logical intervention. To open fire on the military police, and in that exchange of fire to kill perhaps 100 detainees? Maybe that would have been the solution. Maybe I would have been more satisfied in that case. Excuse me, maybe that would have been to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just, you mentioned that there was no established line between the military police outside and inside. Does that mean that the military police could also go inside and practice the same actions; and vice versa, that you can go outside and do whatever you like if there was no -- if there was no established line?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. I am referring to the people who were escorting the buses, who had taken those detainees into custody, and they were the ones who took them off the buses and put them up in appropriate rooms. This is what I'm talking about. So they could also entered the premises at that moment until that work of putting up prisoners was completed. They were able to enter the actual premises. There was no way of preventing them from entering those buildings. There were no instructions or orders to that effect, that that would have been prohibited. The military police came to ask for some detainees on several occasions, the detainees that they wanted to interrogate on the matters that were of interest for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And if they entered inside and did this and practised the same violations, asking them to beat each other, as you said, or that -- did you have the authority to stop them, or were they higher than you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, at that moment they were above us. It was upon -- up to the guard who saw that to decide whether he would intervene or not, and it depended on the attitude he had with the military police. It was something that depended on every individual guard. I told you about myself. I would have intervened had I been present down there when that happened. So it is an individual thing, whether to oppose the military police or not, and it depended on the assessment of each guard of the situation. And when I was in a position to make such an assessment, I would do that. If it was impossible for me to do anything, at least I would comment on what was going on or tell people it is really not an appropriate thing to do, please stop it, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, did you use the same line of reasoning when persons were getting off the bus and you described the heroic intervention of stepping in front of what you described to be a drunken Serb with a machine-gun who subsequently killed, is it four, five, or six people? Did you do the same analysis of in whose custody these people were before you intervened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was thinking along the same lines, only this was a very drastic example because of the noise and the shooting that took place. I stepped over that threshold, if can put it that way. I reacted in accordance with my principles as a police officer. And here, as I told you, it was a matter of singing songs. I don't think it was life threatening in any way, although I know it's a kind of humiliation, and the detainees probably experienced it as a humiliation. But their lives were not threatened, and their lives would have been threatened if there was -- there had been an intervention and a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe we were talking -- or Mr. Reid was asking you about people being beaten, not singing. Does that change your opinion about the need to intervene and invoke -- or cast away what you said were rules and use your police instincts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't change anything. As I said a moment ago, in addition to singing, the prisoners were made to slap each other on a couple of occasions. I don't think that slaps are life threatening. But again, I have to say that it was my assessment. Had I interfered, had I entered into a conflict with the military police, shooting might have occurred, and the people from the escort would have probably opened fire and some people would have been killed. If you analyse the situation, you are presented with a choice of two evils. You choose the lesser one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a little bit about the description of your job before, just before the wartime situation in Omarska transformed your department as you then knew it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher would be kind enough to distribute 3/206.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The document before you, 3/206, is -- does everyone have it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My document is in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have one in Serbo-Croat. Let me give it to you, please. Do you have it in your language now, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The document is out of Sarajevo from January of 1990, and it is called "Rules on the Internal Organisation of the Republican Secretariat of the Interior." This, at one time, this secretariat, would have been your parent organisation, would it not, your umbrella organisation? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. On the English page 2, there's a paragraph number 40 which is labelled, "Duties and tasks of the patrol sector leader and the patrol area leader." You were a patrol sector leader in the Omarska Police Station Department and then the Omarska Police Station; that's correct? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was the leader of the patrol sector within the Omarska Police Station Department. As regards the police station in Prijedor, I was one of the patrol sector leaders later on, until 1993. After 1993, I was also a sector leader in Prijedor in 1994, and after 1994, I was the shift leader in Prijedor. But that all happened in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. The patrol sector leader position was Omarska, then, is that correct, when you were working at Omarska? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the police station department in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just up to the time of, let's say, April 30th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Very good. Looking at what is included in your job description, and I'll just take a few points so as to -- I'm sure everyone can read it, but "establishes a security dossier for the area/sector; responsible for ensuring that data in it is kept up-to-date; patrols the sector/area and performs preventive, operational, and repressive duties and tasks in the sector/area; constantly evaluates the security situation in local communes in the sector and informs the station commander and proposes measures for every newly arisen situation," and it goes on and on. This type of job description reflects your understanding of what you would have been doing as a patrol sector leader; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So these would have been your responsibilities on the eve of the takeover of Prijedor; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were my regular tasks, not responsibilities, the tasks that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are carried out by a patrol sector leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for confirming that. Now, when you -- excuse me. If we were to try to get a very vague idea -- not so much a vague idea but a notion of the responsibilities, the job responsibilities of, let's say, Zeljko Meakic, would that include seeing how policemen were working? I mean, in a supervisory role, seeing how policemen were working, how they were doing, using experience to suggest the correct way of conducting themselves, would that be something that Meakic should have been responsible for as well? Does that sound like his role?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at the time he was the commander of the department?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, and the camp. I mean, would that be fair to say, that he had among his duties, drawing on his experience, to observe how the policemen were working? Would that be your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been expected, that he would, in a way, supervise the work of the policemen; that is, a department commander would supervise the work of police officers, in professional terms. However, as regards the actual command structure, that wouldn't really mean anything, except for the fact that it would involve the drafting of the daily schedule. You have two things here: You have the command structure and the professional structure. You can have a position in accordance with the command structure and you can also have a position because of your professional abilities. The commander of the department is there because of his professional skills; however, he receives orders from the police station commander. Everything relating to the commanding itself comes from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: His experience and skills would enable him, if he noticed something not correct with his troops, with his subordinates, to correct it or to inform them of the need to correct their behaviour; would that also describe something that Meakic would do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been necessary for him, to correct certain irregularities, to give his advice. If he was not able to do that, then in that case, he would have to refer the matter to his superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
