utterances.text: On page 39 of your interview with Investigator Reid, and that would be in Serbo-Croat, 43 and 44, that is, 43 and 44, with the English being 39, Reid puts to you the question:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you do in the camp? What was your role? What did you do during the time that you were in the Omarska Interrogations Centre, your day-to-day duties?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Zeljko Meakic was not there, and I already said that I did not have a guard post which I was supposed to be at, his orders, so to say, to me meant that I was to see how the policemen were working, how they were doing; to use my experience and suggest to the policemen the correct way of conducting themselves; and probably if I noticed anything wrong, to inform him. That would be the essence of it. That sounds very much like what you just described Mr. Meakic would be doing. I would also like to ask you about the amount of time that you --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to comment. Yes, but you seem to be looking for something else and moving over. First of all, this may sound similar, but that was the task of Mr. Meakic in respect of his subordinate policemen. On the same page you have the question, "When Mr. Meakic is issuing you a task, is he issuing you the task as his subordinate policeman or as his deputy"? and the answer is, "As his subordinate police officer," and it goes on and on. It is my obligation, as an experienced policeman, to give suggestions to a less-experienced police officer, especially a reserve police officer. We are talking about reserve police officers here. They do not know anything about the work of the police. They had only recently joined the force. It is my obligation, without specific orders from Meakic, to provide them with appropriate suggestions and advice. But I probably took it to mean quite literally and exaggerated a little bit. It would have been far better for me to have moved away. And I think that more evil would have been done, more harm would have been done in that way, but I wouldn't be considered as a superior. But we are talking about sector leaders here who are at that position because of their professional abilities and not because of the command structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The number of hours that you were at work, we touched on yesterday, and I didn't think it was clear. If I understood you, you suggested that of the hours that you spent, a significant number were spent in the office. How many hours a day did you spend in the office when you were on shift?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very hard to tell exactly now. I said that for the first two days I was there something like 16 or 18 hours. Maybe yesterday I said 19. But, anyway, 16 or 17 hours was the time I spent in the investigation centre during the first two days. Out of that, half the time in the office. We've already said that that morning Zeljko told me to continue my duty shift until he tells me to stop, and I did. On the way -- and he also mentioned the fact that there was some new reserve policemen. "Be there for them so that they don't do something wrong," those were Zeljko's orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Page 97 of your interview with Bob Reid, which in Serbo-Croat would be 102, 102 roughly, you are asked by Reid:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On an average, as best you can, can you estimate how long you were doing this out on the pista area, down in this area in the carpark, in the restaurant, occasionally in this area here, on average how many hours a day would you be doing that in a 12-hour shift?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was all the time. If I was there for 12 hours, that was the total time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That you spent outside?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would go into the office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many hours in a shift would you spend in the office?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we put all the time together as I went in an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The other 10 to 11 hours, you were outside somewhere in the centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that. So if the lion's share of your time, if the majority of your time were outside, did you see, did you hear people suffering? Did you see persons lying on the pista on a regular basis in the heat? Did you hear screams?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard screams when I was in the office. I explained that yesterday. I don't want to repeat myself and waste time. I saw them lying down on the pista once, and I told you about that yesterday. I won't repeat myself. I did see men, and in view of the conditions and the situation, they were suffering. But I didn't see how they were suffering. I saw people with injuries. But you must take something else into account: I spent there from the 28th or the 29th, I don't remember the exact date, most probably from the 29th in the morning until the 22nd or 23rd of June. For two or three days, three days I was off after that incident, and I was also off between the 16th and the 19th because of problems with my left leg. I can show you those injuries which are still visible if necessary. So I was absent for six days, and taking into account the shifts when I was replaced by others. So please build into your questions the actual time I spent there, four or five nights and maybe another six, seven, or eight days. I can't work it out now mathematically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your interview with Bennett --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your interview that is marked "Bennett Interview" has a question on English page 4, a question which is put to you in the lower half of the page, question, "Did you try to have members of your family" -- oh, I'm so sorry. I thought you had it. Do you have it in front of you, Mr. Kvocka. It's a question about --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you try to have members of your family or your wife's family who were in Omarska released?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain that to you. I did not try to have them released. For they also had been brought to the investigation centre and I thought that if they were guilty of anything in connection with the organising of the attack on the Serbian authorities in Prijedor, they should undergo the procedure, but for the sake of providing for their security when I was absent I put them up with my parents near the camp, the investigations centre. In your interview with Mr. Reid on English page 139, which would be in your language --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the objection, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this text was quoted from by Ms. Somers yesterday. She's quoting from it again. Mr. Kvocka has explained, and again she's referring to another text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, did you hear Ms. Susan Somers' question? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, wait, then. Please put your question, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On your page 138/139 in the Serbo-Croat text of your statement, you said -- let's see now. I beg your pardon. I'm sorry, it's 147, I'm wrong, 147 of the Serbo-Croat text. The discussion is about your brothers-in law, and it begins on the bottom of English page 138, and then continuing on to 139 you say, it's in answer to the previous question, "No, not at that time. But I did go to see Simo Drljaca to ask him to release them. I believe I even went twice, but I did go once for sure. He was very brief and told me that he did not want to discuss this with me and that he was not going to release any Muslims and told me to leave his office." My question is, which is the truth? Did you ask for the release, or didn't you? Just so I can know which one to believe.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the truth. I told Bob Reid that, and I said it in my testimony. I also said that to Mr. Chris. Chris didn't ask me whether I asked for their release. I said that I could not release them because somebody had decided that they go into detention. And the person who made that decision could release him. And as it appeared to Simo Drljaca who decided on the detention of persons, I didn't know at the time who was the one. It was a regular procedure: the chief up to three days, then the investigating judge, and so on. We talked about that the day before yesterday. However, Chris asked me why I didn't release them, and I said that I could not release them. If a competent authority had decided to put them in detention, then as a policeman, I have to respect that decision. There is not something that I can do to rescind that decision. But after the interrogation by the investigators who did the interrogations of my brothers-in-law, and as those guys are quite good guys, Neso Babic and Neso Tomcic, they said that they had no guilt of any kind and that everything was fine, but that that was the end of their job. And once I heard that, Meakic told me, "Don't ask me to go to Simo. You know what he's like. You go and talk to him since they have been interrogated and no guilt has been established." And then after that, I went to see Simo Drljaca. So I could not release them, I could only protect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I'm sorry for interrupting you. Mr. Simic, please, could you stand up. What is your objection now?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these questions were covered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, this is the first time that Ms. Susan Somers is asking the witness which is the truth because she compared one version with another version. Do you understand that, Mr. Simic? Do you accept that your intervention was precipitous?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You may be seated. Ms. Susan Somers, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You just said something I wish I could ask you for an explanation on: "So I could not release them, I could only protect them." How could you protect them? Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the way I did. If I repeat all that, that will be taking up your time. I could protect them by violating a particular rule, taking them out of the premises which had been designated for the detention of persons. You have the orders among your documents when Simo Drljaca says that no one can be released without his signature. Regardless of the staff and the investigators and the coordinators, that nobody could release a prisoner without his signature. You have that among your documents. So I took a risk in this case. It's becoming a bit boring and quite embarrassing for me to keep emphasising something I did, so I don't like to talk about it, but I did that out of my human considerations and moral considerations. I didn't pay attention to what would follow. I am aware of the confusion in the investigation centre and around it, and I know that all kinds of things could have happened to them and all the others. And to avoid that and to simply rid myself of some pressure, if I put them in my house, I have more time for the others. If I had left them there, then I would have guarded them only. And then some other people would have been left unprotected that I wanted to protect. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wanted to protect everyone, in fact, but possibilities ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you visited Trnopolje to release your in-laws or to get at least one of them released, did you also --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two of them, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you also pass Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's possible to pass it, that's why I hesitated, but no. You can -- you would have to go through the town and the road along the rail tracks. You don't take the road towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you came in from your home in Prijedor going to work, did you pass Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the time of the existence of the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When it was an active --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, then no. While the Keraterm camp was functioning, I had to go to work via Gomjenica, Cela, Tomasica, but this was not on a daily basis because I spent some nights in Omarska. I would go to Prijedor to check on my apartment, sometimes from midnight until morning. On one occasion we tried, but before the Keraterm camp was established. This was immediately after the operations in Kozarac as far as I can remember. There was a military police checkpoint there and there was no traffic, so I was turned back. After that, I didn't even try to go that way. Maybe one could have passed, but so as not to waste time and have to turn back, the next few times that I went there I took the road via Tomasica, Cela -- Gomjenica, Cela, and Tomasica, and then to the left, the road to Donja Maricka, and that is how you reach Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So do I understand that when you went from Prijedor to Tukovi, you don't pass Keraterm? You don't pass it, is that -- just so I understand the directions, you would not pass it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're mentioning Tukovi for the first time now. I explained to you yesterday that Tukovi were on the road from Prijedor to Sanski Most, and Keraterm is on the road from Prijedor to Banja Luka. These are two opposite directions in relation to the town of Prijedor. If you're going to Sanski Most you pass through Tukovi, and when you're going to Banja Luka, you pass by Keraterm. And when you're going to Omarska, the Omarska camp, there are two or, in fact, three ways of going there. Going past Keraterm along the Prijedor-Banja Luka railway tracks when you pass through Trnopolje, and the Gomjenica-Cela road, and you turn left to Omarska just before reaching Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you didn't go to the intersection of the crossroads where Keraterm is found, you did not go that route? Even though it would have been along the main road, you found another route?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was going to Omarska? Yes, in that period. I did go later on. I don't know whether Keraterm was already dismantled by then. Afterwards, that road to Omarska was open.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated yesterday, made a comment about Simo Drljaca hating you. What is that based on? Why would he hate you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use the word "hate." I said that he ignored me. He ignored me because of my first encounter with him which was an unpleasant one, so I concluded from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher would be kind enough to distribute 3/207.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] The English version is with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document is only in the English language as that is the language of the individual who sent it in, and I will have to rely on the translators -- the interpreters to assist us from the ELMO. This document was drafted and sent by a Colonel Jozsef Boda, a Hungarian national, who is in his own country at this time as a training officer, but in 1996, from March until end of December, was working for the International Police Task Force, commonly known as IPTF, in the Banja Luka district region, in the office there. He performed his duties as a deputy regional commander and then became regional commander. Colonel Boda indicates that, in the course of his duties with IPTF, at the end of March, he received a poster on indictees that was circulating in Bosnia-Herzegovina. IPTF, and I shall quote, "We started an investigation and tried to identify the war criminals in our area of responsibility. We successfully identified four war criminals in Prijedor area." The first is listed as Miroslav Kvocka; the second, Milojica Kos --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My client is presumed innocent until proven guilty. He is described in this document as a war criminal. That violates the Statute of this Tribunal. It should not be before the Chamber. It violates his right to the presumption of innocence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Not yet. [Interpretation] Yes, now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The terminology is not what is critical here, Your Honour. It is a person whose first language is not English. However, it is evident that the poster involved is the IPT -- the ICTY poster which is distributed worldwide. What is the crux of this document is what was done by Simo Drljaca in the next paragraph. The characterisation, I think that would go to weight. Certainly counsel is correct that perhaps "indictee" would be more appropriate, but we did not write this, we received it. And I think that if permitted to proceed on the next paragraph, having simply set the stage to show the link to this trial, if the Chamber would let me proceed and understand what this is about, that would be helpful. I think I can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we are not here with any prejudices. These are words that are used which shouldn't be used. In any event, the Chamber is not to make similar conclusions simply because that is what it says in this document. This is rather like what Judge Wald said a moment ago. Mr. Fila, you also have an observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any objection. But I got a document which must have been given to me by mistake. I have three pages, Your Honour, and this is the third page signed Selina. I'm sorry, I forgot my glasses so I cannot read the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is a two-page document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I have consists of two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But mine has three, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are lucky. You are luckier than me, Mr. Fila. Perhaps Ms. Susan Somers can check with the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So is that all, Mr. Fila? Fine. Ms. Susan Somers is very generous. She gave you three pages instead of two. Please proceed, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I ask the Chamber to allow me to thank Mr. Fila for his assistance in returning it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I inquire, is this a document which comes out of the documents you've had admitted into evidence - I note its very recent origin - or is this just something you're using again for the purposes of cross-examination but not for admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document came specially. It is not part of any seizure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that because it's 12/02/2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's correct. This document is a confirmation of certain information that was sent to us as recently as yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. But are you - are you - just using it now for the purpose we talked about earlier, as a basis at the end of which you'll say, "What do you think about that, Mr. Kvocka?" or are you going to, at some point, attempt to introduce it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In fact, I was going to attempt to introduce it, albeit I don't have the individual here at this time. But, reading between the lines, I can certainly read from it the relevant portions. It would be, however, my intention at some point - if not now, then on rebuttal - to introduce it. But I would like to at least have the opportunity to address the central issues to the witness, and depending on answers, seek to move it into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you're not seeking --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to, subject to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You're not seeking to admit it right now. If you are, then we do have the authentication problem. This is like affidavits for us. If you have an affidavit problem, then you've got to have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm mindful of that. I would just ask it to be identified with a number and held in abeyance. But I would like, if the Chamber permits me, to ask questions from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Boda indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, in my view, you can't admit it now. You would have to go through the regular procedures as with affidavits. I guess you can ask questions from it, but I think that it is a somewhat prejudicial document to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may ask just:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From the description of the individuals, without characterising at all, the individuals mentioned in this document, if I may, Your Honours, by IPTF are Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mirko Babic, and Mladen Radic. The issue is a request made by IPTF to the Chief of Police, Simo Drljaca, in Prijedor, to provide the duty schedule of different duty officers. In so doing, it became apparent that Miroslav Kvocka, that you were working at the Prijedor Police Station or Police Department. When Mr. Drljaca was requested to take action to arrest, it was denied, it was refused. Are you aware -- can you give us any reason why Simo Drljaca would refuse, as a police officer, to assist you in any way if he distrusted you, disliked you, or, as I recollect from the language you used yesterday, hated you? Why would Drljaca, if you can guess, do that, or did he do that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I start guessing, I have to understand your question correctly. What did he refuse, how he protected me, how he didn't protect me, what it is that the international policeman asked for, I'm afraid I don't understand anything from what you said. Who refused to do what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were working under Simo Drljaca after you had been indicted by this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was chief of the centre. At the end of 1995 or the beginning of 1996, there was a reorganisation in the security service of the whole republic, and he was still the chief. But from 1993 until 1995, he did not work, he did not work in the police in Prijedor. But he was brought back in 1995 or 1996. I don't know the exact date, but those were, roughly, the years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: He was aware, was he not, of the fact that you had been indicted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume he did. Everybody knew about it when they heard it on the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you explain why you, as a policeman, having heard about it, and why he, as your superior officer, knowing about it and being a sworn police officer, refused to honour the warrants of this Tribunal and hand you and your other colleagues under indictment over for arrest?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first place, he didn't want to surrender because he too was indicted secretly; not in public, that is true. But according to my reasoning, all these things that we've been talking about for the last four or five days, with Bob Reid for four or five days, with you for these three or four days, all these are reasons why Simo Drljaca would prefer to kill me than to deliver me to the international police. He was protecting himself not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca, I believe, was indicted in 1997. Did he ever discuss with you concerns about indictment? Did you two ever talk about indictment together?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on one occasion he said, "I won't be seen going to The Hague dead." I remember what he said. That is precisely why I told Chris Bennett that I would sort of even like to be arrested but that I did not want to surrender to The Hague. I wanted it to look like an arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Whether or not he was under indictment at the time, and I cannot say for certainty the date, did the two of you have an agreement about not surrendering and possibly encouraging others not to do so, for example, Kos, Radic? Was there any agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have any contact, the two of us. I did work for awhile after the indictment in the service, and it was probably during that period of time, Simo told me, "I won't be seen going to The Hague dead." If I had given him any indication that I would go, I don't think I would have ever arrived here. If I had indicated to him or, rather, intimated to him that I would go to The Hague, I don't think that I would have ever gotten here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the yard of my house - I call it my house but it's actually the house of my in-laws, the parents of my wife - in the garden. I was wearing very dirty boots, torn trousers, and my wife wanted me to put on my shoes but they wouldn't let me, though I raised my hands immediately. But those people were very excited. As they were handcuffing me, their hands were shaking, and with those three words of English that I knew at that time, I said, "It's okay. Everything is going to be fine. Do not be afraid." I wasn't afraid of anything except perhaps of their fear, the fear that they demonstrated. I was afraid that they might fire a bullet into my head or into my wife or my daughter, to whom they placed a gun at the doorstep of our house. They were holding a gun against their forehead like this. I wanted everything to be done as smoothly as possible so that the neighbours wouldn't have to watch this scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you resign from the police or were you decertified?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sacked. Actually, I was told that I could no longer come to work. It was sometime in October or November of 1996, I believe. But then after awhile, the then chief of police, that is, the second man after Simo Drljaca, told me that the best thing for me to do would be to sign a termination of employment by mutual consent. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So after awhile, he sent me a document to that effect and it was, officially speaking, by mutual consent that I terminated my employment there. But that piece of paper was signed probably one month after I stopped working, and he very briefly explained to me that the IPTF would no longer allow for me to work in the police. So it was actually not my desire to leave the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you still getting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you still receiving a police pension or salary now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Currently, the situation is not really resolved. It's not clear. I could have retired earlier on. I had already fulfilled all the necessary criteria for early retirement. But I still felt capable of continuing with my work and my service, and I didn't make any mistakes in my work, so I didn't think that they could, that they could force me to retire. Because that was the kind of thing that was commonly used in the police: If anyone committed a mistake, he would be forced to retire. I am sure that there are members of the police service who would be -- who would gladly have me back in the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Somers. I don't think that you have used all of the time that was allotted to you. Thank you very much. Shall we start with additional questions, Mr. Simic? Are you ready to proceed? But I think that you have already used 20 minutes of your time. No, it's -- I'm not serious. I was referring to the 20 minutes that you used of the Prosecutor's time, but no, I'm just joking. You have all the time you need for your additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, yesterday in response to a question by Ms. Somers that was put to you regarding brigades and other terrorist organisations which were mentioned in the context of your work in the embassy in Paris, I should like to ask you several questions in relation to that matter. How many people were providing security to our embassy in Paris?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three men. There were always two officers. I know that from the preparations that we had at the time. But the situation in Paris was somewhat special and specific because the immigration, both Ustasha and Chetnik immigration in France was very strong at the time. So that was the main reason, not because of any other foreign terrorist organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said three men were employed there. How were the shifts organised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, two of these three individuals had to be there during the working hours of the embassy. They had to be present there in a room which was next to the entrance to the building, and the third would be off during that period of time. However, once -- after the working hours of the embassy, one officer always had to be inside the building of the embassy, and the other two could go out, were free to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you describe your typical day of work in the embassy in Paris?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be sitting in one of the offices. That office had a TV monitor from which we could control the entrance into the embassy. Later on there was an x-ray machine which was set up there in that office, and with that x-ray machine we could control the contents of smaller shipments like letters or similar parcels. That was all. We supervised entry of individuals into the embassy, but that was a very -- that was a very easy part of our job because our citizens were the most frequent visitors. They visited the consular premises; however, when it comes to the embassy, our usual guests were diplomats, people you do not really suspect, you assume that they are clear, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: What aspect of police work would your job in Paris constitute? What kind of police work is that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We discussed the issue of uniforms that you wore at length, and I should like you to clarify some things for us. Mr. Kvocka, what kinds of uniforms did you yourself wear while you worked as a member of the duty service in the Security Service of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only wore the regular blue police uniform which was commonly used by the police at the time, that is, a light blue shirt, sometimes with short sleeves sometimes with long sleeves, it depended; and a pair of trousers which were somewhat darker, greyish or bluish, made of special kind of tissue called kangar. There was also a blue jacket to go with the uniform if the weather was cold. And on a few occasions, I also had a green camouflage uniform which resembles a military camouflage uniform 99 per cent; however, there is a small difference because of the material it is made of. I can explain that to you if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask for the Exhibit number 34/1 to be shown to the witness. D34/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, do you recognise these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. These are the uniforms that belong to the police with the usual police insignia. You cannot see the trousers, but this is the kind of blue shirt that I wore for about 15 years while I was in service.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you wear that shirt in the Omarska camp as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I also had this insignia, but I think I only -- I had three stripes here on the epaulette. This is what you get every four years, for every four years of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask the usher to show the witness -- we can remove this exhibit and have 3/81 shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, before I ask my question, could you please identify these people for me?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can identify two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who can you identify on this picture?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first individual here that we can see on the photograph and the tallest one is Simo Drljaca. Next to him is a person I don't know, and behind him, this small person, the small guy, is Zeljko Meakic. And this man here is a man with a beard, I'm not quite sure who that person might be. But I'm sure about these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, have a look at the uniforms worn by Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you have that kind of uniform on those two or three occasions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for that small difference that I told you about, I think that my wife told you about that. She made this uniform of a special material which has some yellow hue in it. So there is a very small difference between this type of uniform and the one that I had a couple of times. But more or less you can say that it is the same kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the background on which we can see this pattern, is it the same colour?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a green background, the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We can remove that photograph. 3/81 -- I'm sorry, 3/22, if we can have that document at hand, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, yesterday in your testimony you said that when you first arrived in Omarska, that is, to the investigation centre or the camp, whatever you prefer, you told us that on that occasion you found members of the military police there who were wearing uniforms which you saw for the first time on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you have a look at this photograph now, please. Members of the units whom you found there at that time, did they have this kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, those several policemen whom I was able to see in the morning. That is, I never saw anyone wearing any other kind of uniform. Those who were there all had this uniform with blue background and light and darker spots or pattern. You cannot see it very well on your screen, but it is quite visible on the photograph. It was a blue uniform with darker and lighter spots on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer need the photograph, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, while you were in the investigation centre in Omarska, did you ever wear this kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, these uniforms, did they -- were they ever used by the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received it at the end of 1994, beginning of 1995, for the first time when all police officers were wearing this type of uniform. It was at that time that it became the official uniform. Before that, it would appear from time to time on members of special units or intervention platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I don't think an introduction is necessary, both you and many other people told us about the presence of a Special Police Unit in Omarska at the beginning. Could you tell us about the kind of uniforms that they wore?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group who was there during the first week was wearing various kinds of uniforms. The second group which was under the command of Strazivuk, all of its members had this type of blue uniform that we have just seen, and they had a number on their sleeves, 1, 2, 3. Those were some kinds of insignia that they had which indicated to the membership of their unit or to a larger portion of their organisation -- I'm not familiar with their structure. The only thing I can say was that they had this very large number on their sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, we have heard a number of testimonies here of witnesses who said that they had seen you in Omarska in this blue uniform, the one that we identified on exhibit number 3/22. Could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a serious comment on that. It's a lie. I never put on a blue camouflage police uniform before 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kvocka, we talked a lot about the police station department. I should like you to describe for us the building itself, that is, the building of the police station department in Omarska and what it consisted of.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The department was located in a building, I cannot tell you exactly how big it was. It had two entrances and it was a one-storey building. There were two entrances on the ground floor. I can tell you about why there was a second entrance; I'm familiar with the situation. But it consisted of a whole room which was used by duty officers, and then another room which was used by police officers in general, and there was a third room which was used by the commander of the department. So those were the premises which were used by the police station department. There was a partition wall there as well which separated that area from the area with the second entrance that I mentioned. From time to time, this second portion, second half of the ground floor, was used as a flat which was allocated to a police officer who didn't have a flat. This was also customary before I arrived. There were also two other spaces upstairs for the police -- that were intended for the police originally. But I know that a war veteran from the Second World War used to live there and also a policeman who -- a retired policeman who used to work there before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I think that this would be a convenient moment for a break. You were not going to finish within five minutes anyway so we might as well have a lunch break at this point. A 50-minute break, please. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.56 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Simic, we have had ten minutes of sun so you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, when you were describing the building in which the police station department of Omarska was headquartered, you mentioned the duty room. Could you please tell us what the purpose of that room was and who would be in that room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One or several duty officers would be in that room, depending on the daily schedule drawn up by the commander. The function of the room is to have a telephone and a radio communications device. Occasionally, there would be a TV set, a radio. All citizens, if they had anything to report, would come to that room. That would be the description.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: If the leader of patrol sectors, together with their partners, were to go to carry out an assignment in their sector, upon their return, would they report to the duty officers that they had come back?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is where they returned to. They leave their reports with the duty officer, because we would usually come late, after the working hours of the commander, so that the commander would see them the next day. The rule is, however, if the commander is present, that he should send us on assignment and see us when we come back. But the duty officer will then make a record of the fact that we had returned from our patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: During your testimony and the testimony of many witnesses, mention was made of the duty room of the security service in the Omarska investigations centre. Could you describe the contents of that room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a point, it resembled the duty room in the police station department, insofar as there were one or several duty officers there. There was a radio communications device and a telephone, which wasn't really operating too well. The other part of the duty room was occupied, so to speak, by others so that it didn't perform its normal function, because there were two typists additionally working there, and I think we heard about all that from witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, according to the Rules of Service, which you mentioned frequently here, is it allowed or advisable for other persons to be present in the duty room apart from officers on duty? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to the rules, there should be only one or several duty officers there, precisely because if citizens had something to report, they can report it to the duty officer without anyone else being present. That is why I am saying that the duty room was degraded, in a sense, in the investigations centre because of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know who designated that particular room as a room to be used by duty officers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that it had already been designated as such before we arrived. Whether it was by the commander of the Prijedor Police Station or by whoever it was who issued the order on the establishment of the investigations centre, I'm not sure. But somebody from that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: When members of the police station department took over the security service, was that room, duty room, technically equipped?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The radio station already existed; there was a telephone probably from before. The radio station was installed for that purpose, but before we arrived, it was already operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, upstairs in the administration building, was there a room where interrogations were not conducted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of the corridor that you would face directly, there was a door leading to a room where there was no interrogation, as far as I know. That is where the bosses, the coordinators, whatever they were called in the various documents, were there; and people if they came to visit. I said somewhere, either in my testimony or to Bob Reid, that I once saw through the open door of the duty office Simo Drljaca going directly into that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did you ever enter that room where the coordinators linked to the three different lines of investigations were sitting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: The duties of the duty officer, did they differ from the duties providing security from the standpoint of someone who is familiar with the functioning of the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a visible difference in the way in which duties are performed. A duty officer is on duty in a room where he has a desk and a radio receiver, whereas a security service officer either performs guard duty in a particular place if he is assigned to do so, or by patrolling a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can that give an impression of differences in status or position among people who are not familiar with the work of the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Various terms were used by people in free speech, and I remember from my own practice when I would come home after patrolling on foot with mud up to my knees and tired, and I walk into the duty office and say, "You're having an easy time, Chief. You're sitting in a dry and warm room and watching television." So this is a just a manner of speaking that we would use addressing one another. But in fact, that policeman may have only just started working as a policeman, but I would still address him as "chief" because his position was much better than mine. But of course, the word is used ironically.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, my learned friend a moment ago showed you a document marked 3/206.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could I ask the usher to be returned to Mr. Kvocka. It is the rules on the internal organisation of the republican secretariat for internal affairs. Could the usher place the second page on the ELMO where it says, "Duties and tasks of the patrol sector leader and the patrol area leader."

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, my learned friend quoted from this document paragraph 40, "Duties and tasks of the patrol sector leader and the patrol area leader," and she quoted certain tasks which you recognised as falling within your duties. However, I will not go into that now, though she left out some of those duties, but I would like us to clarify something else. It says towards the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you move the page up, please, Mr. Usher so that we can see the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: It says here, "Duties and tasks of basic activities," and then "- specialised - operational - simple." Mr. Kvocka, in police practice, the patrol sector leaders' duties, were they considered to be simple duties as defined by the rules?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. These are considered to be the simpler activities within the police service. These are considered simpler activities. That is regulated by decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You testified today that you were the patrol sector leader until 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need those documents any more. Mr. Kvocka, yesterday in answer to one of Ms. Somers' questions, you mentioned an incident in which, as you put it, a petty criminal took part known as Djordjin. You also testified that you saw this from the window of the duty office?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: How far was it between your room and the place where the incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to make a kind of semicircle covering a distance of some 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You also testified yesterday that in the compound there were other security officers. So let me ask you now, were there any in the corridor in front of the duty office and the office of the inspectors?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some guards, because almost always there were some guards in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you order one of the guards to carry out this duty of camp commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give orders to anyone. All that I can do is what comes under the description of the tasks and duties of a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did any one of the guards, other members of the security, come to your assistance?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, during your testimony, you mentioned a person by the name of Igor Kondic several times.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said that during one visit you found him in a very bad state, because he had been beaten up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask Mr. Kvocka to be shown a document, and distribute it to Their Honours and the parties. It is D44/1, if admitted, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Have you received the document? Mr. Kvocka, will you look at the second page where you see photographs of several persons.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You see that it says there, "Igor Kondic."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is that the person that you mentioned in your testimony, saying that you found him in a very bad state after he had been beaten up on one of your visits?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent, that is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, could you read what newspaper this was published in and on what date?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The name of the newspaper is Kozarski Vjesnik; the date, the 7th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I should now like to ask you to look at the top left-hand corner of the obituary to Mr. Kondic and read out what it says.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 7th of August 1992 it will be 40 days from the premature death of our beloved and never forgotten son and brother, Igor Kondic," then the date when he was born and the date he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: According to our local customs, is this the 40 days that is always observed when somebody dies?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think among Orthodox believers, 40 days after the death of a person, there is a religious ceremony, the tomb is visited, and friends and family are informed about that ceremony through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Mr. Igor Kondic had died 40 days prior to this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here with precision. The ceremony was on the 7th of August, and that date marks the 40 days since his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did you see Mr. Kondic when you brought your brothers-in-law there or during a visit? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to visit them for the second time, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The document will no longer be needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, a great deal of time was spent here in an effort to explain the status of a police station department. My learned friend presented a document marked 3/186. It is the work schedule for the 18th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I register an objection, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The death of Igor Kondic was not an issue that was raised during the course of the cross. I don't want to make an unwarranted objection, but if there is any issue specifically about this individual, I just want to remind the Chamber it did not come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, what is the question that was raised in the cross-examination that you wish to clarify with the help of this document? In other words, will you respond to this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will respond very clearly. Your Honours, 70 per cent of the cross-examination by my learned friend had not been included in the examination-in-chief. You yourself said that there was a certain degree of flexibility allowed in this Chamber, and this was a point that we wished to clarify as there is an affidavit and a protected witness who testified about this. So I think the same amount of flexibility should apply to the Defence, though we will not take advantage of it very much in our re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that the difference, Your Honour, is that we have, under 90(H), the obligation to put the case, the entire case to the witness not just the limited questions that are raised on direct. In so doing, we've had to put all the evidence that has been presented. Our cross, as I read the Rules, unless I have misread them, would be limited by -- our counsel would be limited by the scope of cross in that 90(H) talks of putting the case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Simic, we have to end this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, your objection is overruled. So you may continue, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to document 3/186. Mr. Kvocka, what does the document in front of you represent?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a customary schedule of work for a particular day which is drawn up in the Prijedor Police Station or any police station. So in the basic police institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is this the general police station which had three departments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, it is the general police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, could you please look at a part of this work schedule for the 18th of May, 1991, where it says "Security Service, order number 417." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Are there nine names listed there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Are members of the department of the Omarska Police Station listed there as well; if so, will you read out their names, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not among the first five, they're not from Omarska, and then the following four are from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, this is a document that we had problems with the translation, so this is on page 2. I don't know whether this was shown to Your Honours. Will you turn over the page, please, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Are those the names, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under number six, seven, eight, and nine, these are policemen from the Omarska Police Station Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you please look and see who issued this work schedule for the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The station commander, Fikret Kadiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Beneath your names, do you find also Police Station Department Kozarac, Police Station Department Ljubija, and Police Station Omarska, and next to Omarska you have the number five?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the schedule that is drawn up by the commander of the police station, for that day he noted all the services provided, and for the departments he just mentioned the number. However, for Omarska, he reduced the number by four because they had already been assigned to some particular service, and the remaining five were probably left at the disposal of the department commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you were an employee of the Omarska Police Station department. How can someone else give you a work schedule for that day without your commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's no one else. He is my main -- he is my commander, Fikret Kadiric. He is the one who makes the schedules for all the workers. But this shows that those remaining in the department, probably because of assignments he had previously given to the department commanders. We have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already heard that the department commander would go to the station commander every morning to be given instructions. So the commander of the police station is the basic commander and the only commanding officer. The others are superiors in a sense, but they do not have the right to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: To make this quite clear, will you please give us the structure of the chain of command starting from you yourself upwards.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all there is the department commander. And then up the chain of command the deputy of the station commander and the station commander himself. Then also the assistant station commanders are my superiors in the chain of command. Their rank is more or less equal to that of department commander. I have also left out, before the deputy and the station commanders there are the shift leaders in the station, and they, too, are superior to us ordinary policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, it seems to me that we've already seen this with diagrams. You have already tendered into evidence these tables with the command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for reminding me. I am aware of that, but I wanted, through Mr. Kvocka's testimony and this document, to illustrate once and for all the police station department, that it wasn't autonomous or independent in any sense but only a small segment of the police station. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I know it's hard, but could you remember what you were securing then at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the number of people envisaged, a total of nine in this case; and in view of the person who was patrol leader at the time, probably Dusan Jankovic, and who was at the time deputy to Fikret Kadiric; and in view of the hours, that is, from 1900 hours onwards, it could have been a football match of the local club Rudar which is -- which often attracts between 5.000 and 10.000 spectators. So taking these elements into consideration, that would be my conclusion, but I can't guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Talking about these things, you mentioned Fikret Kadiric, and yesterday Ms. Somers spoke about him and put some questions to you linked to him. When this report was written, what did it represent?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, 1991, it was written by the station commander Fikret Kadiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And you said a moment ago that Dusan Jankovic was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: After the establishment of three-party rule, SDS, SDA, and HDZ, were there changes in the command structure? What position did Mr. Kadiric hold when he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the elections there were certain rotations, but at the time he was arrested, Fikret Kadiric was commander of the police station for traffic safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And who became the commander of the general police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, was that how the police was organised until the Serbs took over power on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there a change of your commander then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the takeover, the command structure was changed again.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was your commander after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Prijedor Police Station was Cadjo Milutin, and Jankovic took over as chief of police, second in command to Simo Drljaca. So he was chief of all the police in the municipality, but only the uniformed police. That is why the official title is chief "for" the police, not "of" the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go on now to a document, 3/186. The document was tendered by my learned colleague. 3/176. Could the document please be shown. Mr. Kvocka - can we have the document placed on the ELMO, please - in front of you is a document and I would like you to tell us who is the author of this document. What is the origin of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Public Security Station Prijedor, Police Station Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, are we talking about the same police station which also had the police station department of Omarska as its component part?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report of the results of the work of the Prijedor Police Station employees for the purposes of giving out salaries. It was drafted pursuant to a proposal which was discussed at the general meeting and which was signed by the president of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, a police station department, is it also comprised -- is it also mentioned in this report issued by the Police Station Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All three departments are included in this report, that is, the part of the police station of Prijedor, that is, the Ljubija, Kozarac, and Omarska departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you omitted to indicate the period of time for which this report was made.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of June to 15th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please turn to page 3. Here we read "Omarska Police Station Department." Mr. Kvocka, 12 employees are listed here. Were all of them employees of the Omarska Police Station Department?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, but not all of them were actually working within the department during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which of these individuals worked in the Omarska Police Station Department directly, and also the individuals who were relocated and tell us where they were reassigned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to answer your question, as far as I remember. As regards Miroslav Kvocka, yes, but not until the end of this period of time, the period of time for which the salary is calculated. Ljuban Grahovac did not work in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went to the reserve police force in Lamovita. Zeljko Meakic, he worked in Omarska, yes; Branislav Bojic as well. Bozo Karajica did not work in Omarska. I think that he went to the reserve police in Prijedor, the area of Urije. Dusan Aleksic, if this is Dusko whom I know, went to Rakelici. Mladjo Radic, he worked in Omarska. Boro Delic also worked in Omarska. Branko Mudrinic went to Prijedor as well, to the Urije section, to the reserve police force there. Dragan Macura did not work in Omarska at that time, but I don't know exactly where he went. Milutin Bujic, he went to Rakelici; that was what he himself told us the other day. And, finally, Zeljko Stojnic, I don't know exactly where he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, we all heard the testimony of Mr. Bujic here, who told us that in March 1992 he was deployed by Hasan Talundzic to the reserve police station in Rakelici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So how come his name is on the salary list of the Omarska Police Station Department for the period of time from the 16th of June until the 15th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is his original police station, that is, the police station of Prijedor. He had his assignment at the police station department in Omarska, and it is from there that he was redeployed. So this is why he is still mentioned on this piece of paper which is issued by the finance service. This is a salary list. He could not have been on any other salary list.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there a job description within the overall structure of police officer at the reserve police station in Tukovi or Rakelici?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no such possibility provided for in the Rules of Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: While you were working in Tukovi, on what salary list could your name be found at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police station of Prijedor, probably in this section referring to the departments, until a new appropriate decision was issued. I think it was issued in 1993 sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, was this document drawn up by the people who are familiar with the structure and the status of the police at the time, at the time this document was written?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. This document was issued by the Prijedor Police Station and the report was made according to the list of employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is the official term that is used in this document for your work place, that is, for your job in the month of June, at the moment this report was drafted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term that is used is the police department in Omarska. That is the appropriate term. They're using the official document, the right document which is prescribed for in appropriate regulations. "Police Station Department Omarska." So from this title, one can conclude that the department in question is part of a given police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Practically speaking, at the time you left, was that place, the place where you worked, was that the police station department of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me go back to document 3/208 at this point. I no longer need this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, yesterday you had an opportunity to see this document, and throughout these proceedings, I think we all omitted to deal with the issue of members of the military who were part of the internal security service. Please have a look at the Roman numeral one and tell us what this section of the document covers.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Members of the army unit helping out," and then we have 19 individuals listed under this title.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, are these the soldiers the individuals that Nenad Pusac, if I remember it correctly, testified about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novak Pusac, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. These individuals were helping out inside the compound as part of the internal security service. It's a group of soldiers who were helping out the internal security service, that is, the members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were wearing the old JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That can be seen from this document. They were not members of that force.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they have their own superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but I don't know who that was. However, within the structure of the unit itself, there must have been someone, but I don't know exactly who their superior officer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You have had ample opportunity to familiarise yourself with this document. What was the purpose of this document or, rather, of this request?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document actually expresses a wish of Zeljko Meakic to put some order as regards entries into the compound of the investigation centre or the mine complex, as far as I understand it, because one can see that there are over 40 people who were employed there, that is, in the mine company, in various shifts. Then there are also 19 individuals here who were not members of the police, and he probably wanted to have a certain document issued for these people; that is, the members of the military who would be allowed to enter the compound of the investigation centre in order to avoid various individuals wearing uniform or having a military identity card to enter the premises. That happened very often at the beginning. It is my assessment that he wanted to know exactly who can be allowed to enter the investigation centre because he was in charge of the security of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer need the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, and this is something that was also mentioned by your wife and I addressed that issue in my opening statement, mention was made of the fact that you seized some money from Desanka Stanojevic and not Desanka Popovic. I believe I misspoke the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like document D45/1 to be shown at this point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what is the document that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an ordinary document used by members of the police, and it is a certificate for the temporary confiscation of items.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I would like you to be as brief as possible because we are running out of time and tell us what is certified in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document certifies that I, together with two other police officers, had carried out a confiscation of a certain amount of money, the legal tender is indicated here, as well from Desanka Stanojevic from Gornja Omarska, and then the address is given, number BB, on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we get any further, the clarification of the date I would request. The original language suggests it is 13 of the 5th month, and the translation has a question mark next to "March" in English. Is it possible to have some clarification as to which month is invoked here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. I think that we can all read 13th of May 1992, at least this is what I see on the document. But the witness might be able to help us with the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to thank my learned colleague as well. We also had not noticed that there has been a technical mistake here in the translation, but we have the original in front of us, so we're able to clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say that the measure -- the procedure was -- took place on the 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who were these items confiscated from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Desanka Stanojevic, daughter of Aleska, from Gornja Omarska, BB, no number.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
